title: Performative Learning Theory
claim: Predictions that reshape their target population make generalization from a sample uncertain, and the more they change the world, the less can be learned.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, map and people icons then trade-off plot
description: Three side-by-side panels. Panel 1.1 shows a stylized map of the San Francisco Bay Area with colored cars and route pins. A magnifying glass zooms in on San Francisco, and a black curved arrow points from the zoomed city (the sample) to the wider Bay Area (the population). Panel 1.2 shows a large oval for the German population, containing a smaller inner oval for Bavaria. Both ovals hold rows of emoji-style workers, some in hard hats and some looking worried. In the inner oval, a red arrow runs from the unemployed to a job-center building, and the outcome shows more workers in hard hats. In the outer oval, the same arrow ends in a large question mark. A big curved arrow points from the inner oval to the outer one. Panel 1.3 is a line plot of the generalization gap bound against the share of job seekers receiving training. A blue total bound rises, an orange performative term rises, a green complexity term falls, and a red sampling term stays flat at zero.
caption: 1.1 Example (A): Route predictions are known to have performative effects: Drivers avoid routes with predicted congestion, thereby rendering these predictions less accurate. Can routing apps still generalize from San Francisco (sample) to the whole Bay Area (population)? 1.2 Example (B): A job center in Bavaria assigns job training programs to those among the unemployed that have high risks of long-term unemployment according to machine learning (ML) predictions. As a result of the job training, their probability of finding a job increases, a textbook example of a performative effect, see Section [ref]. Can the job center's ML model trained on performatively shifted data from Bavaria generalize to the whole German population, which will in turn react to the predictions? 1.3 Theorem [ref] applied to job seeker data: Growth of generalization gap bound (blue) shows trade-off between performatively changing a population (by assigning more people to job trainings) and reliably learning its properties. Details on the bound's components (red, green, yellow) are in Section [ref].
abstract: Performative predictions influence the very outcomes they aim to forecast. We study performative predictions that affect a sample (e.g., only existing users of an app) and/or the whole population (e.g., all potential app users). This raises the question of how well models generalize under performativity. For example, how well can we draw insights about new app users based on existing users when both of them react to the app's predictions? We address this question by embedding performative predictions into statistical learning theory. We prove generalization bounds under performative effects on the sample, on the population, and on both. A key intuition behind our proofs is that in the worst case, the population negates predictions, while the sample deceptively fulfills them. We cast such self-negating and self-fulfilling predictions as min-max and min-min risk functionals in Wasserstein space, respectively. Our analysis reveals a fundamental trade-off between performatively changing the world and learning from it: the more a model affects data, the less it can learn from it. Moreover, our analysis results in a surprising insight on how to improve generalization guarantees by retraining on performatively distorted samples. We illustrate our bounds in a case study on prediction-informed assignments of unemployed German residents to job trainings, drawing upon administrative labor market records from 1975 to 2017 in Germany.
